query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys reported to date commonly contain both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Induction-melted Al- and Mg-rich alloys reached densities of 2.64–2.75 g/cm3 but all had complex structures; Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 combined a density of 3.91 g/cm3 with 911 HV hardness and oxidation resistance at 700 and 900 °C; compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd showed region-dependent compression, plasticity, and corrosion behavior; and reported AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys contained a primary BCC constituent together with intermetallic compounds, with x = 1.0 showing the best property combination in that series. Prior studies have emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, whereas interfacial segregation, interfacial energy, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance remain insufficiently studied. The design must retain a density below 6 g/cm3 and address performance constraints associated with the tendency of Mg and dissimilar constituent elements to form stable intermetallic compounds. Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state, what single intervention hypothesis could improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance? State the intervention, its proposed causal mechanism, quantitative or directional predictions relative to the as-processed baseline, the composition and operating or test boundaries, the prior experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with explicit observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Addition of Cr to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys improves combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Cr2Ta Laves phase and Cr2O3 oxide layer
generation.mechanism: Cr and Ta have strong binding ability, forming Cr2Ta, and Cr diffusion rate is faster than Ta, enabling Cr2O3 formation, which improves oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance
generation.uncertainty: Optimal Cr content and processing conditions for maximum performance improvement

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment with varying Cr content and processing conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If addition of Cr does not improve combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Intervention effect. Base system: WVTaTiCr x coatings. Intervention: Varying Cr content (0 to 10.08 wt%). Processing: Laser cladding on 42-CrMo steel; powder mixed by ball milling (300 r/min, 10:1 ratio, 24 h). Test conditions: SEM/EDS analysis of cross-section and surface morphology after oxidation. Structure change: Ta and W concentrated in dendrites; V and Cr enriched in interdendritic regions; Laves phase (Cr2Ta) forms network in interdendritic areas. Property change: Oxidation resistance improves with Cr; corrosion resistance improves with Cr; hardness increases with Cr. Mechanism: Cr and Ta have strong binding ability (enthalpy of mixing −7 KJ/mol) forming Cr2Ta; Cr diffusion rate faster than Ta, enabling Cr2O3 formation. Evidence: measured. Quote: "Ta and W with high melting points are first solidified and formed, and mainly distributed in the white dendrite area; there is a high content of V and Cr elements in the gray area."

Intervention effect. Base system: HfMoTaTiZr alloy. Intervention: Addition of 4.2 at% Cr. Processing: Vacuum arc melting. Test conditions: Room temperature. Structure change: Laves phase formed due to Cr reacting with Ti, Zr, Hf, and Ta. Property change: Hardness increased by 56.96% compared to reference. Mechanism: Hard intermetallic Laves phase and solid solution hardening. Evidence: measured. Quote: "We speculated that the formation of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZr 0.5 is attributed to the fact that Cr can form various Laves phases with the constituent elements in HfMoTaTiZr such as Ti, Zr, Hf, and Ta."
